messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Politician
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Military Topics: Talks about military, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nadim is a 64-year-old American man of Middle Eastern background, divorced, now serving in public office after many years in humanitarian work. He traces the beginning of his current difficulties to a relief deployment in a war zone several years ago, when he was coordinating aid deliveries in a civilian district that had already been emptied by shelling and repeated fighting. He remembers the day in fragments rather than as a single continuous story. There had been a lull that morning, the kind of strange quiet that people around him had learned not to trust. He had been moving between a damaged building being used for supplies and the street outside, speaking with people he did not know well, trying to work out who still needed food, medicine, and transport. What returns to him most sharply is not a full sequence but pieces: the silence feeling wrong, someone approaching to talk, the air changing, and then the smell of burning. When he tries to tell it, he reaches a point where the terror arrives in his body as if it is happening again and he has to stop speaking.

In the snippets he can describe, there was a sudden blast nearby, confusion in the street, smoke and heat, and people shouting over one another. He recalls trying to orient himself while the burnt smell thickened around him, unable at first to tell where the danger was coming from or who had been hit. He remembers faces only in flashes, voices without names, and the sense that every person moving toward him might be carrying urgent news or fresh threat. The memory does not sit in his mind as a settled account. Instead it breaks apart into disconnected pieces that do not fit together, and when one piece comes back—especially the smell, or the moment just before the noise, when everything had gone unnaturally still—he is flooded by the same fear he felt then.

After he returned to the United States, Nadim tried to live as though discipline would be enough. He did not want to be seen, especially in political life, as a man ruled by feeling. He had come to believe that if he let himself fully feel what was there, he might lose control in public or become unable to function. So he worked hard to contain himself. When distress rose, he redirected his attention immediately: another call, another briefing, another policy memo, another meeting. Throwing himself into work felt safer than pausing. In the years since entering politics, this has only become easier to justify. Long hours at the office, constant travel, and packed schedules give him ready-made ways to keep his mind occupied.

Still, the world narrows around certain moments. Talking to strangers can unsettle him in ways he finds hard to explain. Much of his job requires shaking hands, listening to unfamiliar constituents, and fielding spontaneous approaches in hallways, campaign events, and public receptions. When someone he does not know steps in close to ask a question, he feels himself tense and begins taking in details of posture, hands, exits, and who is standing where. He does the same when conversations turn to military matters. Even routine policy discussions about troop movements, defense funding, or conflict overseas can leave him abruptly distant and vigilant, as if part of him has been pulled back to that street. The smell of something burnt—a scorched appliance in an office kitchen, overheated wiring at a venue, char from a city street food cart—can stop him cold before he can tell himself where he really is.

What unsettles him most in daily life is how quickly danger seems to gather in silence. If a room goes unusually quiet, he feels certain something is about to happen. He scans automatically: windows, doors, corners, people’s expressions, the nearest route out. At home, this has become a nightly ritual of checking locks and rechecking them, then circling back again because certainty does not last. In hotel rooms during campaign travel, he inspects doors and windows before he can settle, sometimes more than once. He knows this appears excessive, yet it feels irresponsible not to do it. In his mind, vigilance is what keeps catastrophe from arriving unannounced.

The cost has become increasingly visible. Staff have noticed that he can seem abruptly preoccupied in meetings, especially if a visitor enters unexpectedly or a discussion turns to war. He stays later than anyone else, often under the banner of dedication, though privately he knows he is also avoiding the unstructured quiet of going home. His divorce is long-standing and not something he links to one cause, but he lives with a marked sense of isolation now; there are few places where he lets himself stop performing steadiness. He finally sought help after becoming overwhelmed during a public conversation on foreign affairs when a question from an unfamiliar audience member, followed by extended silence in the room, left him struggling to continue. What frightened him most was not simply the memory itself but the possibility that he could no longer keep it contained. At the same time, he is hoping for some way to speak about what happened without being seized by the same terror, and to move through his work and private life without always bracing for danger.
